verses.t: Gaozi said, "Human nature is like the willow, and righteousness is like a cup or bowl. To make benevolence and righteousness out of human nature is like making cups and bowls out of willow wood." Mencius said, "Can you make cups and bowls by following the nature of the willow? Or must you first do violence to the willow and only then make cups and bowls of it? If you must do violence to the willow to make cups and bowls, must you also do violence to people to make them benevolent and righteous? Surely it would be these words of yours that lead everyone in the world to regard benevolence and righteousness as a calamity!"

Gaozi said, "Human nature is like swirling water. Open a channel to the east and it flows east; open a channel to the west and it flows west. Human nature is indifferent to good and not good, just as water is indifferent to east and west." Mencius said, "Water is indeed indifferent to east and west, but is it indifferent to up and down? The goodness of human nature is like the tendency of water to flow downward. There is no person who is not good, just as there is no water that does not flow downward. Now, by striking water and making it splash, you can make it go over your forehead; by damming and channeling it, you can make it stay on a hill. But is this the nature of water? It is the force applied that makes it so. When people can be made to do what is not good, their nature is being treated in the same way."

Gaozi said, "What is inborn is what is called nature." Mencius said, "Is saying that what is inborn is called nature like saying that what is white is called white?" "Yes." "Is the whiteness of a white feather like the whiteness of white snow, and the whiteness of white snow like the whiteness of white jade?" "Yes." "Then is the nature of a dog like the nature of an ox, and the nature of an ox like the nature of a man?"

Gaozi said, "Appetite for food and sex is nature. Benevolence is internal, not external; righteousness is external, not internal." Mencius said, "Why do you say benevolence is internal and righteousness external?" "When someone is older than I am and I treat him as an elder, the elderliness is not something in me. It is like something being white and my calling it white because its whiteness is outside me. That is why I call it external." Mencius said, "There is no difference between the whiteness of a white horse and the whiteness of a white man. But is there no difference between the elderliness of an old horse and the elderliness of an old man? And is it the one who is elder that is righteous, or the one who treats him as an elder?" Gaozi said, "My own younger brother I love; the younger brother of a man from Qin I do not love. Here the feeling depends on me, so I call it internal. I treat an elder from Chu as an elder, and I also treat my own elder as an elder. Here the feeling depends on age, so I call it external." Mencius said, "My liking for roast meat from a man of Qin is no different from my liking for my own roast meat. The same holds for other things. Is our liking for roast meat, then, also external?"

Meng Jizi asked Gongduzi, "Why do you say that righteousness is internal?" "It is the expression of my respect, so I call it internal." "If a villager is a year older than your eldest brother, whom do you respect?" "My brother." "When pouring wine, whom do you serve first?" "The villager." "So the one you respect is here, but the one you treat as elder is there. It really is external and does not come from within." Gongduzi could not answer and told Mencius. Mencius said, "Ask him, 'Do you respect your uncle or your younger brother?' He will say, 'My uncle.' Say, 'If your younger brother is impersonating the ancestor at a sacrifice, whom do you respect?' He will say, 'My younger brother.' Say, 'Where then is your respect for your uncle?' He will say, 'It is because of the position he occupies.' Then you too can say, 'It is because of the position he occupies. My ordinary respect goes to my elder brother; my momentary respect goes to the villager.'" When Jizi heard this, he said, "When I am to respect my uncle, I respect him; when I am to respect my younger brother, I respect him. So it really is external and does not come from within." Gongduzi said, "In winter we drink hot water, and in summer we drink cold water. Is eating and drinking, then, also external?"

Gongduzi said, "Gaozi says, 'Human nature is neither good nor bad.' Some say, 'Human nature can be made good or made bad. So when Kings Wen and Wu arose, the people loved goodness; when Kings You and Li arose, the people loved violence.' Others say, 'Some natures are good and some are bad. So with Yao as ruler there was still Xiang; with the Blind Man as father there was still Shun; with Zhou as their elder brother's son and their ruler as well, there were still Qi, Viscount of Wei, and Prince Bi Gan.' Now you say that human nature is good. Are all of them wrong, then?" Mencius said, "As far as its genuine condition goes, it can become good. That is what I mean by calling it good. If people do what is not good, it is not the fault of their native endowment. The heart of compassion all people have; the heart of shame and dislike all people have; the heart of respect and reverence all people have; the heart that approves and disapproves all people have. The heart of compassion is benevolence; the heart of shame and dislike is righteousness; the heart of respect and reverence is propriety; the heart that approves and disapproves is wisdom. Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom are not welded onto me from outside; I have them in me already. It is only that I do not reflect on them. Hence it is said, 'Seek and you will get it; let go and you will lose it.' Some differ from others by twice, five times, or countless times, because they have failed to make full use of their endowment. The Ode says, 'Heaven gave birth to the multitudes of people; where there is a thing, there is a rule. The people hold to their constant nature, and love this admirable virtue.' Confucius said, 'The one who wrote this ode understood the Way! Where there is a thing there must be a rule; the people hold to their constant nature, and so they love this admirable virtue.'"

Mencius said, "In years of plenty most young men are dependable; in years of dearth most young men are violent. It is not that Heaven endows them so differently, but that something has entrapped and drowned their hearts. Take barley: you sow the seed and cover it with soil; the ground is the same and the time of planting is the same; it springs up vigorously, and by the summer solstice it is all ripe. If there are differences, it is because the soil is rich or poor, and the nourishment of rain and dew and the work of the farmers are unequal. So all things of the same kind are alike. Why should we doubt it only when it comes to human beings? The sage and I are of the same kind. Thus Longzi said, 'Even if someone makes sandals without knowing the size of the feet, I know he will not make baskets.' Sandals are all alike because the feet of everyone in the world are alike. Mouths have the same likings in flavor, and Yi Ya was simply the first to discover what my mouth likes. If the nature of the mouth in regard to flavor differed from person to person, as dogs and horses differ in kind from us, why would everyone in the world follow Yi Ya in their taste? When it comes to flavor, the whole world looks to Yi Ya; this shows that everyone's mouth is alike. It is the same with the ear. When it comes to sound, the whole world looks to Music Master Kuang; this shows that everyone's ear is alike. It is the same with the eye. As for Zidu, there is no one in the world who does not know he was handsome; whoever does not know Zidu was handsome has no eyes. Therefore I say: mouths have the same likings in flavor, ears the same hearing in sound, and eyes the same sense of beauty in color. When it comes to the heart, is it alone without anything in common? What is it that hearts have in common? Reason and righteousness. The sage was simply the first to discover what my heart has in common with others. So reason and righteousness please my heart just as the meat of grazing and grain-fed animals pleases my mouth."

Mencius said, "The trees of Ox Mountain were once beautiful. But because the mountain lies on the outskirts of a great city, axes and hatchets chopped them down. Could it remain beautiful? Yet through the rest it had by day and night, and the moisture of rain and dew, it was not without buds and shoots springing up. Then cattle and sheep came to graze on it, and so it became bare as it is now. People see its bareness and think it never had any timber. But is this the nature of the mountain? So too with what is preserved in a person: how could he be without a heart of benevolence and righteousness? The way he lets go of his good heart is like the axes and hatchets against the trees. Chopped down day after day, can it remain beautiful? Through the rest it gets by day and night, and the air of the early dawn, his likes and dislikes come close to those of other people, but only slightly; and then what he does during the day fetters and destroys it again. When it is fettered over and over, the night air is not enough to preserve it; and when the night air is not enough to preserve it, he is not far from a beast. People see that he is like a beast and think he never had any good endowment. But is this a person's genuine condition? So, given proper nourishment, there is nothing that will not grow; deprived of proper nourishment, there is nothing that will not waste away. Confucius said, 'Hold on to it and it stays; let it go and it is lost. It comes and goes at no fixed time, and no one knows where it dwells.' Was he not speaking of the heart?"

Mencius said, "Do not wonder at the king's lack of wisdom. Even the most easily grown thing in the world will never grow if it gets one day of sun and ten days of cold. I see the king very seldom, and when I withdraw, those who chill him arrive. What can I do with the few shoots that appear? Now take the game of go: it is a minor art, but unless you give your whole heart and mind to it you will not master it. Yi Qiu is the best go player in the whole state. Suppose Yi Qiu were teaching two people to play. One gives his whole heart and mind to it and listens only to Yi Qiu. The other, though he listens, is thinking the whole time that a swan is about to fly by, and wants to take his bow and corded arrow and shoot it. Though he studies alongside the first, he will not equal him. Is this because his intelligence is inferior? I say it is not so."

Mencius said, "Fish is something I want; bear's paw is also something I want. If I cannot have both, I will let go of the fish and take the bear's paw. Life is something I want; righteousness is also something I want. If I cannot have both, I will let go of life and take righteousness. Life is something I want, but there is something I want more than life, so I will not cling to life by improper means. Death is something I hate, but there is something I hate more than death, so there are dangers I will not avoid. If there were nothing people wanted more than life, why would they not use any means by which they could stay alive? If there were nothing people hated more than death, why would they not do anything by which they could avoid danger? Yet there are means of staying alive that people will not use, and ways of avoiding danger that they will not take. So there is something people want more than life and something they hate more than death. It is not only the worthy who have this heart; all people have it. The worthy simply do not lose it. Here is a basket of rice and a bowl of soup; get them and you live, go without and you die. If they are given with an insult, even a wayfarer will not accept them; if they are given with a kick, even a beggar will disdain them. Yet when it comes to ten thousand bushels of grain, a man accepts without asking whether it is proper and right. What do ten thousand bushels add to me? Is it for the beauty of my mansions, the service of my wives and concubines, and the gratitude of the needy people I know? What before I would not accept even at the cost of my life, now I accept for the beauty of my mansions; what before I would not accept even at the cost of my life, now I accept for the service of my wives and concubines; what before I would not accept even at the cost of my life, now I accept for the gratitude of the needy people I know. Could this not have been stopped? This is what is called losing one's original heart."

Mencius said, "Benevolence is the human heart; righteousness is the human road. How sad it is when people abandon their road and do not follow it, and let go of their heart and do not know how to seek it! When people's chickens and dogs stray, they know to go after them; but when their heart strays, they do not know to go after it. The way of learning is nothing else than seeking the strayed heart."

Mencius said, "Suppose someone's fourth finger is bent and will not straighten. It is not painful and does not interfere with his work, yet if there were someone who could straighten it, he would not think the road from Qin to Chu too far, because his finger is not like other people's. When his finger is not like other people's, he knows to be troubled by it; when his heart is not like other people's, he does not know to be troubled by it. This is called not knowing the relative importance of things."

Mencius said, "Anyone who wants to grow a tung or catalpa tree that can be spanned with one or two hands knows how to nurture it. But when it comes to their own person, they do not know how to nurture it. Is it that they love their own person less than a tung or catalpa tree? They simply do not think."

Mencius said, "People love every part of their bodies, and since they love every part, they nurture every part. There is not an inch of skin they do not love, so there is not an inch of skin they do not nurture. To judge whether someone is good or not, what other way is there than to see what he chooses for himself? The body has parts that are noble and parts that are base, parts that are small and parts that are great. Do not harm the great for the sake of the small, nor the noble for the sake of the base. One who nurtures the small parts becomes a small man; one who nurtures the great parts becomes a great man. Suppose a gardener neglects his wutong and jia trees and tends his sour jujube and thorn bushes: he is a worthless gardener. One who tends a single finger and loses his shoulder and back without knowing it is a man confused and diseased. People look down on a man who cares only for eating and drinking, because he nurtures the small and loses the great. If a man who cares for eating and drinking lost nothing [greater] by it, would his mouth and belly be merely an inch of skin?"

Gongduzi asked, "All alike are human beings, yet some become great men and some become small men. Why is this?" Mencius said, "Those who follow their great part become great men; those who follow their small part become small men." "All alike are human beings, yet some follow their great part and some their small part. Why is this?" "The organs of the ears and eyes do not think and are obscured by things. When one thing meets another, it simply draws it along. The organ of the heart thinks. If it thinks, it gets it; if it does not think, it does not get it. This is what Heaven has given us. If one first establishes the great part, the small part cannot snatch it away. This is how one becomes a great man, that is all."

Mencius said, "There are noble ranks conferred by Heaven and noble ranks conferred by men. Benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and good faith, and delight in goodness without tiring: these are Heaven's ranks. Duke, minister, and great officer: these are men's ranks. The ancients cultivated Heaven's ranks, and men's ranks followed after them. People today cultivate Heaven's ranks in order to obtain men's ranks, and once they have obtained men's ranks they discard Heaven's ranks. This is the height of delusion, and in the end they are sure to lose everything."

Mencius said, "The desire to be honored is common to all people. Everyone has something in himself worthy of honor, but they do not think of it. The honor that men bestow is not true honor. Those whom Zhao Meng ennobles, Zhao Meng can also debase. The Ode says, 'He has filled us with his wine, he has filled us with his virtue.' This means being filled with benevolence and righteousness, so that one does not covet the taste of other people's fine meat and grain; and a good name and wide fame rest upon one's person, so that one does not covet other people's embroidered robes."

Mencius said, "Benevolence overcomes what is not benevolent as water overcomes fire. Those who practice benevolence today are like someone trying to put out a cartload of burning firewood with a single cup of water; when the fire is not put out, they say that water cannot overcome fire. This goes far toward siding with what is most unbenevolent, and in the end they are sure to lose even what little they have."
Mencius said, "The five grains are the finest of seeds, but if they do not ripen they are worse than wild grasses. Benevolence too depends simply on being brought to ripeness."

Mencius said, "When Yi taught people archery, he always had them aim at drawing the bow to the full, and learners too must aim at drawing the bow to the full. When a master carpenter teaches people, he always uses the compass and square, and learners too must use the compass and square."
